title: Iterating Maps: keySet, values & entrySet
summary: The 3 view collections of a Map: why entrySet() is 2x faster than keySet()+get(), iterating with for-each, forEach() lambdas, and computeIfAbsent().
prerequisites: The Map Contract: Associative Key-Value Storage
learningObjectives: Understand the 3 collection views of a Map: keySet(), values(), and entrySet()
Analyze why entrySet() is 2x faster than keySet() + get() by eliminating secondary hash lookups
Master Java 8 functional idioms: forEach(), computeIfAbsent(), computeIfPresent(), and merge()
Implement high-throughput grouping and aggregation patterns cleanly
expectedOutcomes: Ability to write idiomatically modern, optimal map traversal and aggregation code in enterprise services
Elimination of double-lookup anti-patterns in production Java applications

activities.title: Practical Context: Reading an Invoice with Both Item and Price Simultaneously

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Reading an Invoice with Both Item and Price Simultaneously
analogy.story:
Imagine an accountant reviewing a ledger of 1,000 invoices. In Method A, the accountant reads only the customer ID from the ledger, walks over to the file cabinet, searches the file by ID, retrieves the price, and walks back—repeating this 1,000 times!

In Method B, the accountant opens the invoice binder where each page contains both the customer ID and the price side-by-side (an Entry), reading both in a single pass without any walking.

Method A is keySet() + map.get(k) (requiring 2,000 operations). Method B is entrySet() (requiring exactly 1,000 operations, twice as fast).
analogy.keyTakeaway: entrySet() provides direct access to both key and value in a single traversal, eliminating secondary hash lookups.

keyTakeaways: entrySet() returns Set<Map.Entry<K, V>> giving immediate access to both key and value
Iterating with keySet() followed by map.get(k) is an anti-pattern that doubles hash lookup overhead

questions.question: Why is iterating a Map using entrySet() faster than using keySet() + map.get(key)?
options: Because entrySet() is compiled into native assembly code
Because entrySet() already holds references to both key and value, avoiding a secondary hash computation and bucket lookup for each key
Because keySet() creates a deep copy of the map
questions.explanation: entrySet() directly accesses the Node.key and Node.value fields during iteration. keySet() + map.get() requires hashing the key a second time for every element.

questions.question: What does map.computeIfAbsent(key, mappingFunction) do if the key is already present in the map?
options: It returns the currently mapped value immediately without executing the mappingFunction
questions.explanation: computeIfAbsent is lazy: if the key is already associated with a non-null value, it immediately returns the value and never invokes the mappingFunction.

questions.question: Which method is the most concise way to increment an integer frequency counter in Java 8+?
questions.explanation: map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) inserts 1 if absent, or adds 1 to the existing value if present, in a single atomic line of code.

questions.question: Can you call entry.setValue(newValue) while iterating over map.entrySet()?
options: Yes, setValue() updates the value in the backing map without throwing exceptions
Only if the map is a TreeMap
questions.explanation: Map.Entry.setValue(v) is explicitly defined in the Java Collections contract to update the value in the backing map safely during iteration.

questions.question: How does map.merge() differ from map.putIfAbsent()?
questions.answer: putIfAbsent(k, v) only inserts value v if the key is absent or mapped to null; if the key already exists, it does nothing. In contrast, merge(k, v, remappingFunction) takes an initial value and a BiFunction: if the key is absent, it inserts v; if the key already exists, it applies remappingFunction(oldVal, v) and replaces the old value with the function's result (or removes the entry if the function returns null). This makes merge() ideal for accumulations, counters, and combining states.

questions.question: What is the difference between map.compute() and map.computeIfPresent()?
questions.answer: compute(key, (k, v) -> ...) always executes the remapping function, regardless of whether the key is currently present (v is null if absent). If the function returns null, the key is removed from the map. computeIfPresent(key, (k, v) -> ...), however, only executes if the key is currently mapped to a non-null value; if the key is absent, it does nothing and returns null without invoking the function.

questions.question: How can you safely remove entries during map iteration without causing ConcurrentModificationException?
questions.answer: You can safely remove entries in two standard ways: 1) Using Iterator.remove(): `Iterator<Map.Entry<K, V>> it = map.entrySet().iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { if (condition(it.next())) it.remove(); }`, or 2) In Java 8+, using the entrySet / keySet removeIf method: `map.entrySet().removeIf(entry -> condition(entry));`. Both update internal iterator modification counts safely.

practiceProblems.title: Sum All Values Using entrySet
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement sumAllValues(Map<String, Integer> map) that iterates over entrySet() and returns the total sum of all integer values.

practiceProblems.title: Multi-Map Grouping by First Letter
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement groupByFirstLetter(List<String> words) that returns a Map<Character, List<String>> grouping words by their starting character using computeIfAbsent.

practiceProblems.title: Frequency Counter with merge()
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement countFrequencies(String[] tokens) that returns a Map<String, Integer> counting the frequency of each token using map.merge().

practiceProblems.title: Safe In-Place Entry Removal with removeIf
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement purgeBelowThreshold(Map<String, Integer> scores, int minPassingScore) that uses entrySet().removeIf(...) to remove all entries whose score is < minPassingScore.

practiceProblems.title: Compute Word Length Map
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a List<String> of unique words, use computeIfAbsent or forEach to return a Map<String, Integer> mapping each word to its character length.
